slides.title: What makes prediction different
slides.notes: Everyday predictions: tomorrow's electricity demand, the next bus arrival, where your thumb will be 100 ms from now on a touch screen.

runs.text: Shuffle a set of ECG records and nothing is lost. Shuffle an hour of electricity demand and it becomes meaningless.
The next value depends on the recent past. A plain multilayer network sees only the present input, so the past must be supplied to it.
To predict several steps ahead the network must use its own earlier predictions, and any error in them is carried along.
Prediction is fitting, with the past as the input.

slides.title: Memory from a tapped delay line
slides.notes: From Unit 2: the tapped delay line was introduced with the ADALINE adaptive filter. Here it feeds a nonlinear network.

runs.text: Memory from a tapped delay line
Tapped delay line: the last four values, held side by side
Turn a sequence into ordinary input vectors
A tapped delay line stores the last d values of the signal.
Together they form the input vector for an ordinary multilayer network.
The network is still static; the memory lives in the delay line. This is the focused time-delay network.
How long should d be? Long enough that the errors come out white (L39).

slides.title: The NARX network: past inputs and past outputs
slides.notes: For demand forecasting, u might be temperature and the day of the week, and y the demand.

runs.text: The NARX network: past inputs and past outputs
NARX: nonlinear autoregressive network with exogenous input.
Autoregressive: the output depends on its own past values.
Exogenous input: it also depends on an outside signal u, such as a control current or the weather.
Each has its own tapped delay line feeding one multilayer network.

slides.title: Two ways to feed the output back
slides.notes: This is the standard recipe in the Hagan case study and in the MATLAB toolbox: train open loop, then convert to closed loop.

runs.text: Two ways to feed the output back
The delay line holds the true past values of y.
The network is then purely feedforward, so ordinary backpropagation trains it.
Inputs are accurate, so training is stable.
Feed back the network's own output
The delay line holds the network's earlier predictions.
No measurements are needed, so it can run many steps ahead.
Each small error is fed back and can grow.
Use: multi-step prediction and simulation, after training.
Train in series-parallel form. Close the loop afterwards to predict further ahead.

slides.title: Checking the errors: delay line too short
slides.notes: This is the L39 test applied in the case study. White errors mean nothing predictable is left.

runs.text: Checking the errors: delay line too short
The red errors are still predictable
With a short delay line, an error now makes a similar error likely at the next few steps.
That pattern is information the network could have used.
Lengthen the delay lines and train again: only the spike at lag 0 remains.
Then check the input-error cross-correlation in the same way.

slides.title: Closed loop: errors grow with the horizon
slides.notes: In Finish My Move the closed-loop forecast is the one drawn ahead of the hand; students can see where it peels away from the real movement.

runs.text: Closed loop: errors grow with the horizon
Every forecast has a useful range
One step ahead the network always starts from a measured value, so the error stays small.
In closed loop each prediction is built on earlier predictions, and their errors add up.
Report how far ahead the forecast stays inside the accuracy you need.
Tomorrow's demand is forecast well. Next month's, from the same model, is not.

slides.title: Industry parallel: load and demand forecasting
slides.notes: Special days are the classic difficulty: a festival or a cricket final shifts the evening peak, and there are few past examples to learn from.

runs.text: Industry parallel: load and demand forecasting
A grid operator forecasts tomorrow's demand hour by hour to schedule power plants. Inputs: recent load, temperature, day of the week, holidays.
A grocery app forecasts tomorrow's orders for each neighbourhood to stock its stores. Too little loses sales; too much is thrown away.
Delay lines on the series and on outside inputs, trained one step ahead, checked for white errors, then run forward.
Forecasts are judged in money: every unit of error is fuel burnt, stock wasted or a customer lost.

slides.title: Concept drift: when the world moves on
slides.notes: Concept drift is extrapolation in time. Monitoring is the fifth box of the design flow, "Use and watch".

runs.text: Concept drift: when the world moves on
A good model does not stay good
For eight weeks the live error matches the test error.
Then something changes: summer arrives, prices rise, a competitor opens. The error creeps upward.
The model has not changed. The relationship it learnt has.
Track the live error, set a trigger, and retrain on recent data when it is crossed.

slides.title: Beat the model
slides.notes: People usually win on rounds with a visible event the model has no input for, and lose on steady stretches. That is the lesson on choosing inputs.

runs.text: Show the last 30 values of a real series, such as hourly city temperature or daily match scores.
Everyone writes down their guess for the next value. Then reveal the network's forecast, then the truth.
Score ten rounds: mean absolute error for the class average, the best student and the network.
On which rounds did people beat the network, and what did they know that it did not?
Finish My Move: play the Beat the model round and compare scores.
